title: Gimlet Labs raises $300M at $3B for multi-silicon inference cloud
subtitle: The Andreessen Horowitz-led round funds an inference stack that splits each model across whichever chip runs each phase fastest.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Gimlet Labs closed a $300 million Series B on September 4 at a $3 billion post-money valuation, bringing total funding to $392 million. Andreessen Horowitz led the round, joined by Sapphire Ventures, M12, Arm, Menlo Ventures, and Factory. Gimlet's product, released commercially in March, disaggregates AI inference so different phases of a model — prefill, decode, attention, tool-use — can run on whichever silicon serves each phase best, whether Nvidia, AMD, Intel, Arm, Cerebras, or d-Matrix.

The reason multi-silicon inference is interesting now is that agentic workloads have made the classic single-chip runtime look wasteful. An agent turn is not a single forward pass — it is a burst of long-context prefill, a stream of short decodes, several tool calls with their own runtimes, and often a re-plan. Different steps benefit from different memory bandwidth, cache sizes, and interconnect. Gimlet's pitch is that customers are leaving 30–50% of throughput on the table by pinning an entire agent to one chip family.

The financial signal is what a16z was willing to pay: $3 billion for a company whose first commercial product is roughly six months old. Gimlet has disclosed that one of the top three frontier labs and one of the top three hyperscalers are already customers, and that it has billions in contracted revenue. If those disclosures hold under IPO-grade scrutiny — the company is not close to that yet — the multiple is defensible. If they compress, this becomes a cautionary reminder about how much of AI valuation is now priced off contracted-not-realized revenue.

For learners: agentic inference is where the next round of infrastructure differentiation is happening. If you are early-career and want to work on AI systems rather than models, look at the runtime layer — inference schedulers, KV-cache managers, tool-call orchestration, multi-chip routing. That is where the interesting engineering is now, and where companies like Gimlet are hiring.
